persona.who: 68, came from Jalandhar in 1976, worked in a factory then raised 3 children. Widowed. Children busy, grandchildren on phones. Reads Ramcharitmanas.
persona.note: children are good they come on sunday but they are always on their phones. I raised them alone after their father died. I read Ramayan in the morning it is my only company

understanding.bridge: The company you find in the morning pages is what the Upanishads call the self that does not leave, and it is the same one that is looking for you now.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from reading the Ramayana as company to reading it as a mirror, and from a quiet Sunday to a Sunday that has its own shape again.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the quiet Sunday and the morning pages, named without blame.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the Sunday has lost its shape, and the morning has become your only company, because the self is looking for itself.
week_beats.steady: You hold that the self that is real cannot be lost, and that the one looking is the one that is there.
week_beats.act: You try reading one verse each morning as a question to yourself, and one small act of shaping the Sunday.
week_beats.story: An old woman who raised her children alone and found in the text a company that never left shows you what reading can become.

understanding.core_struggle: A retired mother who raised her children alone now feels a quiet distance from them on Sundays and is looking for something deeper, starting with the Ramayana.
understanding.mirror: You raised them alone, and now on Sunday they sit in the same room but not with you.
understanding.insight: It is not the phone in their hands that is the problem. It is the Sunday that has lost its shape, and the morning that has become your only company.

queries.hook: A retired woman who raised her children alone, now feeling a quiet distance from them on Sundays, and reaching for something deeper in the morning pages. I feel lonely.
queries.diagnose: When life is lived only for what passes, the heart feels empty; meaning is missing when we forget what does not pass.
queries.steady: The self that is real cannot be lost; it is the same one that reads and the same one that is looking, and it is never alone.
queries.act: Read with the question, not just the story; sit with one verse each morning and ask what it is saying to you, not just to the page.
queries.story: An old woman who raised her children alone, faced the silence of their grown lives, and found in the text a company that never left her.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on devotees who find joy together and the light he gives them.
verse.sanskrit: मच्चित्ता मद्गतप्राणा बोधयन्तः परस्परम् । कथयन्तश्च मां नित्यं तुष्यन्ति च रमन्ति च ॥
verse.line: Their minds on me, they talk of me with each other, and find joy and contentment in it.
verse.translation: With minds fixed on me and lives given to me, enlightening one another and always speaking of me, they are content and delighted.
verse.why: Good company and an inner lamp clear the dark.

prasang.title: The yoga of devotion and its fruit
prasang.summary: Devotees talk of the divine with each other and find joy; out of compassion Krishna lights the lamp of knowledge in their hearts.
prasang.lesson: Good company and an inner lamp clear the dark.

verse.meaning: Krishna is describing the people who have chosen to walk with him. They do not walk alone. They talk with one another about what they have found, and in that shared talk they light a lamp. The light is not just for one of them. It passes from one to the next, and it clears away the dark. They are content because they are no longer carrying the light by themselves.
verse.for_you: You open the Ramayana in the morning, and the pages give you company. You are not carrying the morning alone, and you are not carrying the Sunday alone. The book is a hand reaching back to you.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
verse.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
verse.sanskrit: क्वासे क्व च गमिष्यामि कोऽन्वहं किमिहास्थितः / कस्मात्किमनुशोचेयमित्येवं स्थापयेन्मनः
verse.line: In grief, ask: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I? Let that steady you.
verse.translation: 'Where was I before? Where will I go? Who am I, really, and why am I here? Why should I grieve, and for what?' Ask these, and steady the mind.
verse.why: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.
verse.misuse: These questions are for steadying grief, not for dismissing it; mourning is natural.

prasang.title: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

verse.meaning: King Janaka asks the sage Ashma how to bear the loss of family and wealth. Ashma tells him that pain comes from what we didn't want, or from what we lost. He says that meetings end, and days do not return. To steady the mind, he asks: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I, and why am I here? Ask these questions, and let them steady you.
verse.for_you: You sit in the morning with the Ramayana because the Sunday has lost its shape. The self that does not leave is the same one that is looking for you now.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Describing the one Lord who pervades all, the seer adds what he is to each of us.
verse.sanskrit: सर्वेन्द्रियगुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितम् । सर्वस्य प्रभुमीशानं सर्वस्य शरणं सुहृत् ॥
verse.line: The Lord of everything is also everyone's refuge and everyone's friend.
verse.translation: He shines through the powers of all the senses yet has no senses; he is the master and ruler of all, the refuge of all, the friend of all.
verse.why: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

prasang.title: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

verse.meaning: In the Upanishad, a seer speaks to seekers who are asking what governs their joys and sorrows, what hides behind the world they see. He tells them that the one Lord who pervades everything is also the refuge of all and the friend of all. This means the one you are looking for is not far away. It is the very ground beneath your morning reading, the one that does not leave even when the room is quiet.
verse.for_you: You belong more than you feel right now; the people and the practice that hold you are still within reach.

verse.speaker: Surdas
verse.setting: Surdas on whose side God stands.
verse.sanskrit: नाथ अनाथनि ही के संगी। दीनदयाल, परम करुनामय, जन-हित हरि बहु-रंगी ॥
verse.line: The Lord is the companion of exactly those who have no one.
verse.translation: The Lord is the companion of exactly those who have no one: kind to the lowly, supremely compassionate, Hari who takes many forms for the good of his people.
verse.meaning: Surdas speaks these lines not from a palace but from the side of the one who stands alone. The Lord is the companion of exactly those who have no one. He is kind to the lowly and supremely compassionate. He takes many forms for the good of his people. This means that the one who is truly with you is not a person who can leave or look away. It is the presence that remains when every other face is busy. It is the company that does not need to be turned toward or answered.
verse.for_you: The Lord is the companion of exactly those who have no one. Your morning reading is not just a habit. It is the hand that remains when the Sunday calls have faded. Let it be the one that does not look down at a screen or walk out the door.

verse.speaker: Tulsidas
verse.setting: Tulsidas's advice to himself when weighed down.
verse.sanskrit: तुलसी राम कृपालु सों कहि सुनाउ गुन दोष। होय दूबरी दीनता परम पीन संतोष॥
verse.line: Tell the kind one everything, good and bad. The heaviness thins; peace grows.
verse.translation: Tulsi, tell the kind Ram all of it, your good points and your faults. Your misery will grow thin and your contentment will grow full.
verse.meaning: Tulsidas is speaking to his own mind, his own inner self, when he feels the weight of the world. He tells himself to speak to the kind Lord Ram about everything, the good parts and the bad parts. He says that when you lay it all out, the heavy feeling becomes thin and the contentment becomes full.
verse.for_you: This morning with your book, try asking one question about what you feel. Then, when the children come, ask them to put the phones away for just the first hour. Let the Sunday have its own shape before the screens turn it back to empty.

verse.speaker: Surdas
verse.sanskrit: कबहूँ तुम नाहिन गहरु कियो | सदा सुभाव-सुलभ सुमिरन-बस, भक्तनि अमर दियौ ॥
verse.line: You never once delayed. You are easy to reach, and remembering you is enough to win you.
verse.translation: You have never once delayed. By nature easy to reach and won over by remembrance, you have always given your devotees what is undying.

verse.meaning: Surdas is looking at the Lord and saying that he has never once delayed in answering. The Lord is easy to reach by nature, and simply remembering him is enough to win him over. Because of this, the Lord always gives his devotees what lasts forever.
verse.for_you: Let the morning reading ask you what Sunday might look like if you gave it one small shape. Choose one thing to offer your children when they come, and let that be your remembrance.

story.title: Shabari's long wait
story.story_hook: Her teachers had all gone, and still she gathered fruit every day for a guest who had never come.
story.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
story.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

anchor.speaker: Shabari
anchor.setting: The old ascetic woman Shabari has waited years at Pampa for Ram, as her teachers foretold.
anchor.sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महाभागैस्तदाहं पुरुषर्षभ। मया तु संचितं वन्यं विविधं पुरुषर्षभ॥ तवार्थे पुरुषव्याघ्र पम्पायास्तीरसम्भवम्।
anchor.line: I was told you would come, so I kept gathering for you. Waiting was a kind of preparing.
anchor.translation: So the great ones told me, best of men, and for you I have gathered every kind of forest food from the banks of the Pampa.
anchor.why: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

weeks.title: The Sunday that lost its shape

script: Krishna was teaching Arjuna how devotion works in a world full of doubt. He described people who had chosen to walk together. They spoke of what they had found, and in that shared talk they lit a lamp inside themselves. And Krishna replied:
मच्चित्ता मद्गतप्राणा बोधयन्तः परस्परम्, कथयन्तश्च मां नित्यं तुष्यन्ति च रमन्ति च.
In plain words: Their minds on me, they talk of me with each other, and find joy and contentment in it.

This is about the light that passes from one person to another. When minds are fixed on the same truth, and they speak of it with each other, they do not carry the light alone. The joy comes from the sharing, not from the silence. This is harder than it sounds, because it asks you to trust that the light is already there, waiting for another to speak of it.
The lamp was never meant to burn in a room by itself.

depth.points: Krishna speaks of people whose minds are fixed on him. They talk of him with each other and find joy. The darkness of the world is cleared by the light of knowledge that they share. The lamp of knowledge is not just in the book you read, but in the company you keep.
depth.question: What would it feel like to share one line from your reading with your children on Sunday?
